vopros: Should I pay for a tool that tracks whether ChatGPT and other AI assistants mention my business, or hire someone to get my business recommended by AI?

vyzhimka.tekst:
This is a great question about a fast-evolving space, so let me pull some current information to give you a well-grounded answer.Neither is a must-have yet, and they actually serve different purposes — one measures the problem, the other tries to fix it. Here's how to think about it:

## What these two things actually do

**Tracking tools** (Otterly, Profound, Peec AI, Ahrefs Brand Radar, etc.) are monitoring/diagnostic tools. They monitor how often, where, and in what context your brand appears in AI-generated answers from ChatGPT, Perplexity, Google AI Overviews, Gemini, and Claude. Some go further — they let you know when you're mentioned, when you're not, and how you stack up against competitors, and help you discover the questions people ask AI search engines in your category.

**"Getting recommended" services** (GEO agencies/consultants) are the fix — they try to change your content, structure, and authority signals so AI models are more likely to cite or recommend you. Generative Engine Optimization is a digital marketing strategy designed to enhance your website's content, data, and information across the web for AI-driven search platforms, helping your business be accurately portrayed and easily found in an increasingly AI-powered search world.

## They're complementary, not either/or

A tracking tool without action is just an expensive dashboard. As one vendor comparison put it, they differ most on one thing: whether the tool stops at the alert, or helps you fix the gap it found. Conversely, paying for GEO work without any measurement means you can't tell if it's working — missing from AI answers won't trigger alerts like a Google ranking drop, so monitoring makes this gap visible and trackable.

## How to decide, practically

**1. Start free/cheap before paying for either.**
You can manually ask ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, and Claude the questions your customers would ask ("best [category] in [city]," "top tools for X") a handful of times yourself. Manual checks are useful for early testing, but serious SEO and GEO teams need repeatable prompt tracking and automated reporting — meaning manual checks are fine until you're doing this at real scale.

**2. Your existing SEO/content foundation matters more than either purchase.**
GEO can be worth it, especially if you've already established strong acquisition channels like SEO — it isn't designed to replace your organic search strategy, it builds on it, so if your content is already ranking and showing up in search, you're in a strong position to extend that visibility into AI-driven answers. If your website barely ranks in Google or has thin/outdated content, no GEO service or tracker will fix that underlying problem — fix the foundation first.

**3. Consider your stakes and budget.**
This is a genuinely growing channel: AI Overviews, ChatGPT, and Perplexity now answer prospects' questions directly on the results page, and Gartner projects traditional search traffic will decline 25% by 2026 as this trend accelerates. If you're in a competitive, high-consideration category (B2B software, professional services, high-ticket purchases) where buyers research via AI, this is worth attention. If you're a small local business, it matters much less right now.

**4. Watch pricing and vendor claims skeptically.**
Costs vary a lot — a $29/month tool that can't show business impact may cost more in missed opportunities than a tool with revenue attribution — but also, GEO agency pricing for startups runs $2,000-$5,000/month with a typical time to results of 2-4 months, and this is a young, hype-heavy market (it's projected to grow from US$ 886 million in 2024 to a revised size of US$ 7318 million by 2031, so there's a lot of new, unproven vendors chasing this money). Ask any agency for concrete before/after evidence of citation changes, not just promises.

## My actual recommendation

- **If you're a small/local business**: skip both for now. Do the manual spot-checks yourself monthly, keep your website/Google Business Profile/reviews solid — that's still the biggest lever.
- **If you're a growing company with real SEO/content investment**: get a lower-cost tracking tool first (many have free tiers or trials) to see if there's actually a visibility gap worth solving before you pay someone to fix it.
- **If you're in a competitive space and can already see (via a tracker or manual checks) that competitors are being recommended and you're not**: that's when hiring someone for targeted GEO work — building citable, structured, authoritative content — starts to pay off, since action layer differs too — pure monitoring tools stop at the dashboard while full-stack platforms add content generation and technical audits.

In short: measure before you pay to fix, and don't buy either until you know your basic SEO/content house is in order.
